title: Rights and Provenance in AI Art
answer: Copyright and trademark, licensing, training data and opt-outs, studio security, and content credentials.

children.name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
children.blurb: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to outputs from generative image, video, and audio models, including questions of authorship, ownership, infringement, and fair use.

children.name: Licensing Synthetic Media
children.blurb: Licensing synthetic media covers the permissions needed to create, distribute, and reuse AI-generated images, video, audio, and text.

children.name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
children.blurb: Training data and opt-outs concern the datasets used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the mechanisms by which artists and rights holders can ask for their work to be excluded.

children.name: Security for Creative Studios
children.blurb: Security for creative studios covers the protection of original artwork, style references, training data, prompts, model weights, and generated outputs from theft, leakage, tampering, or unauthorized reuse.

children.name: Watermarking and Content Credentials
children.blurb: Watermarking and content credentials are mechanisms for marking AI-generated media so that its origin and edit history can be identified.

sections.body: This field covers the legal and practical rules around who can use AI generated images, video, audio, and text, and how that use is recorded. Artificial intelligence is now producing finished commercial work, from advertising stills to background music, and the systems that make that work are being tracked for ownership and permission. Copyright and trademark questions arise when a model outputs something close to an existing character, logo, or style, while licensing synthetic media sets terms for reuse, resale, and modification of machine made content. Training data and opt outs concern whether an artist's prior work was used to teach a model and whether that artist can remove it from future training. Security for creative studios covers protecting unpublished prompts, style references, and client assets from leaking into public models, and watermarking and content credentials are the technical marks that say a file was made by a particular tool or person.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The legal picture is far from settled, and the site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, with no single clear rule for style imitation or training data. Copyright registration for fully machine generated work has been rejected in some jurisdictions, but human assisted AI work can qualify, leaving a line that is still being drawn case by case. Opt out mechanisms exist for some training datasets, but they are not universal, and an artist cannot always know whether their work was used or enforce removal after the fact. Watermarking and content credentials are technically possible, but they can be stripped or compressed away, so they are not yet a reliable proof of origin. Studio security is improving with private models and contract terms, yet no technical measure fully prevents an employee or contractor from leaking a prompt or asset. The honest limit is that rights and provenance are currently a patchwork of contracts, voluntary tools, and early court decisions rather than a stable legal framework.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader trying to understand whether they can claim ownership of an AI image should start with Copyright and Trademark for AI Work, which explains the current legal tests for authorship and infringement. If the goal is to sell or share that image, Licensing Synthetic Media shows how to set terms for reuse and what standard licenses do and do not cover. Training Data and Opt-Outs is the place to go when the question is whether a model was built on someone else's work and how to request removal from future training. Security for Creative Studios addresses the practical risk of prompts, style references, and client files leaking into public tools, and it connects to the legal pages by showing what evidence a studio needs to protect. Watermarking and Content Credentials covers the technical marks that can attach provenance to a file, and it pairs with Licensing Synthetic Media because a license is only useful if the file can be traced back to its terms. Together these pages move from ownership questions, to permission questions, to the technical and physical safeguards that make those permissions enforceable.
